phonemes.desc: From Sanskrit bodhi, “awakening” — the name begins in the Buddha’s own enlightenment-word.
From √dhṛ, “to hold, sustain” — the same root as dharma’s “that which holds”.
The Chinese rendered it 菩提達磨 (Pútídámó); the Japanese, Daruma; the West, Bodhidharma.

pronunciation.note: The name means “awakening-perfection” or “dharma of awakening” — the Indian prince who carried Zen to China.

domains.title: The Dharma of Awakening, First Patriarch
domains.subtitle: The Indian Prince Who Carried Zen to China
domains.lead: Bodhidharma is the First Patriarch of Zen: the Indian prince-turned-monk who crossed the Pamirs to China around 520 CE, sat facing a wall at Shaolin for nine years, and transmitted the Buddha’s wordless teaching outside the scriptures. His legend is the bridge between India and East Asia — and the seed of martial, meditative, and cultural traditions that span the continent.

cards.name: The Wall-Gazing
cards.desc: Nine years facing the wall at Shaolin; the tradition’s image of unmoving resolve — and of the mind’s own wall.

cards.name: The First Patriarch
cards.desc: The twenty-eighth Indian patriarch who became China’s first — the wordless transmission passed through him.

cards.name: Daruma’s Eyes
cards.desc: The legend: he cut off his eyelids in wrath at sleep — and where they fell, tea plants grew. Japan’s doll watches with one eye.

cards.name: The Bone of the Buddha
cards.desc: His only transmission: a bowl, a robe, and a bone — the mind-to-mind seal outside the scriptures.

mythology.lead: Bodhidharma’s mythology is a layer-cake of history and legend: the historical missionary of the early sixth century; the wall-gazer of the Zen records; the Shaolin temple’s patron of the martial arts; and Japan’s round Daruma doll, whose blank eyes you fill in when your wish comes true. The legend grew because the teaching needed a body — and the body it chose was defiant, foreign, and perfectly still.

myths.title: The Crossing to China
myths.text: The Zen records send him to the court of the Liang emperor Wudi — the great Buddhist patron who asks, ‘what is the highest meaning of the holy truth?’ and is told ‘vast emptiness, nothing holy’. The emperor, scandalized, asks who stands before him: ‘Don’t know’, says the future patriarch, and leaves for the north. The dialogue founded the Zen interview-style in a single exchange.

myths.title: Nine Years, One Wall
myths.text: At Shaolin he sat facing a wall nine years; legend adds that in frustration at sleep he cut off his eyelids — and tea, the meditator’s ally, sprang from where they fell. Huike, his future successor, stood in the snow and cut off his own arm to prove his sincerity; Bodhidharma accepted him and transmitted the teaching. The tradition’s founding images are all of this order: resolve measured in what one will lose.

myths.title: The Temple and the Arts
myths.text: The legend that he taught the Shaolin monks exercises to strengthen their meditation — the seed of Shaolin kung fu — belongs to the later layers, but it fixed his place in the martial imagination: the first patriarch as the first master of body-discipline. The Yi Jin Jing muscle-classic attaches itself to his name.

myths.title: The Round Wish-Keeper
myths.text: Japan made him a doll: round as the wall-sitter’s robe, weighted to right itself — nanakorobi yaoki, fall seven times, rise eight. You paint one blank eye when you make a wish, the other when it comes true. The fierce Indian master ended as Japan’s most cheerful household god of perseverance, keeping his scowl and his self-righting bottom.

lore.syncretism: Bodhidharma is the Silk Road made flesh: Indian dharma, Chinese wall, Japanese doll. The Zen lineages count him as the twenty-eighth Indian and first Chinese patriarch — the hinge of the transmission; and the Tibetan traditions remember him (as Bodhidharmottara) among the great siddhas. His defiance of the Liang emperor became the template of the Zen master’s whole pedagogy.
lore.culturalLegacy: He stands at the head of every Zen lineage — Rinzai and Sōtō alike trace the wall; the Shaolin temple’s global fame rests on his legend; and the Daruma doll, with its self-righting scowl, is Japan’s most reproduced folk object. ‘Zen’ as the West knows it begins, by the tradition’s own account, with his ‘don’t know’.
lore.extendedMeditation: Bodhidharma: the name is a doctrine — awakening-holding, the dharma that holds itself awake. Restored plainly, it spans the journey it names: an Indian word, a Chinese wall, a Japanese doll, and the plain letters any reader can hold. Five syllables, one transmission.

sources.name: Transmission of the Lamp (Jingde Record of the Transmission)
Shaolin monastery tradition and the Yi Jin Jing

lore.archaeology: His supposed grave at Kongxiangsi in the Pagoda Forest of Shaolin carries the earliest memorials; the Shaolin steles of the Tang dynasty name him. The Daruma doll’s manufacture is a modern industry, but the blank-eyed scowl descends from the Muromachi portraits.
lore.cult: Zen’s daily liturgy is his transmission: zazen, the wall-facing sitting, is his nine years made practice. The Daruma-fulfilling rite — the eye-painting — is Japan’s most popular domestic vow.
lore.iconography: The fierce, bearded, wide-eyed Indian in a robe, sometimes with the eyelids; or the round-bottomed Daruma, red-robed, scowling, one-eyed. His icon is the stare — the gaze that outlasts the wall.
lore.reception: History of religion uses him as the case-study of a legend accreting around a historical missionary — the scholarly layers (McRae, Faure) are themselves a literature. The martial-arts world venerates him as its founding master; and the Daruma doll made the fierce patriarch the friend of every Japanese child’s new year.
